'''Nicola Scafetta''' is a [[research scientist]] and  at the [[University of Naples Federico II|University of Napoli Federico II]]. He was formerly at the [[Active Cavity Radiometer Irradiance Monitor Satellite|ACRIM]] Lab group and an [[Professors in the United States#Adjunct professor|adjunct assistant professor]] in the physics department at [[Duke University]].<ref name=cv>{{cite web |url=http://www.fel.duke.edu/~scafetta/pdf/CV_NScafetta.pdf |title=Nicola Scafetta, PhD |publisher=[[Duke University]] |access-date=2012-08-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120206075742/http://www.fel.duke.edu/~scafetta/pdf/CV_NScafetta.pdf |archive-date=2012-02-06 }}</ref><ref name=acrim>{{cite web |url=http://acrim.com/staff.htm |title=ACRIM Staff Information: Science and Instrument Team |publisher=ACRIM |access-date=2012-08-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110925020619/http://www.acrim.com/staff.htm |archive-date=2011-09-25 }}</ref> His research interests are in theoretical and [[applied statistics]] and nonlinear models of complex processes.<ref name=cv/> He is notable for having controversial views on [[climate change]].

==Early life and education==
Scafetta was born in Italy. He received a [[Laurea]] in physics from the [[University of Pisa]] in 1997 and a [[Ph.D.]] in physics from the [[University of North Texas]] in 2001.<ref name=cv/> His doctoral thesis was titled ''An entropic approach to the analysis of time series''.<ref>{{cite web |author=Scafetta, Nicola |year=2001 |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc3033/ |title=An entropic approach to the analysis of time series |publisher=[[University of North Texas]] |access-date=2012-08-21}}</ref>

==Career==
Scafetta was a research associate in the electrical and [[computer engineering]] department at [[Duke University]] from 2002 to 2003 and then a research scientist in the physics department from 2003 to 2009.<ref name=cv/> He has been a visiting lecturer at [[Elon University]] and the [[University of North Carolina]].<ref name=cv/> Scafetta was a research associate at the ACRIM Lab group and an adjunct assistant professor in the physics department at Duke University for a few years after 2010.<ref name=cv/> He is currently affiliated with the [[University of Naples Federico II|University of Napoli Federico II]] in [[Naples]], Italy.<ref>{{cite web|title=SCAFETTA NICOLA|url=https://www.docenti.unina.it/#!/professor/4e49434f4c4153434146455454415343464e434c36395432364437303855/riferimenti|website=unina.it|access-date=20 October 2017}}</ref>

He is a member of the [[American Physical Society]], [[American Geophysical Union]] and the [[American Association of Physics Teachers]].<ref name=cv/>

===ACRIM===
Scafetta argues that the total [[solar irradiance]] (TSI) measurements gathered by satellites since 1978 are flawed because the [[Space Shuttle Challenger disaster|Space Shuttle ''Challenger'' disaster]] prevented the timely launching of the [[ACRIM]] 2 satellite, which he worked on, to replace ACRIM 1. This results in a two-year data gap in the ACRIM time series, which scientists bridge with overlapping data from several other satellites. They conclude that  heating from the [[Sun]] did not increase between 1980 and 2002 and does not significantly contribute to the [[global warming|global surface warming]] over that period. Some ACRIM investigators, including principal investigator Richard Willson (Columbia) and Scafetta, disagree and argue for a significant upward trend in average solar luminosity during the two-year data-gap in the ACRIM time series. The Duke University student newspapers report that Scafetta and West's interpretation of Richard Willson's analysis is that "the sun may have minimally contributed about 10 to 30 percent of the 1980-2002 global surface warming."<ref>{{cite web |author=Basgall, Monte |date=September 30, 2005 |url=http://today.duke.edu/2005/09/sunwarm.html |title=Sun's Direct Role in Global Warming May Be Underestimated, Duke Physicists Report |work=Duke Today |access-date=2012-08-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Dean, Ashley |date=October 19, 2005 |url=http://dukechronicle.com/article/hotter-sun-may-affect-global-warming |title=Hotter sun may affect global warming |work=[[The Chronicle (Duke University)|The Chronicle]] |access-date=2012-08-21}}</ref>

===Scientific contributions===
Scafetta developed "Diffusion Entropy Analysis", a method of statistical analysis which distinguishes between [[Lévy flight|Levy Walk]] noises and [[Fractional Brownian motion]] in complex systems.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Scafetta, Nicola |author2=Paolo Grigolini |year=2002 |url=http://www.fel.duke.edu/~scafetta/pdf/PRE36130_02.pdf |title=Scaling detection in time series: diffusion entropy analysis |journal=[[Physical Review E]] |volume=66 |issue=3 |article-number=036130 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.66.036130 |pmid=12366207 |arxiv=cond-mat/0202008 |bibcode=2002PhRvE..66c6130S |s2cid=18679250 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100610080720/http://www.fel.duke.edu/~scafetta/pdf/PRE36130_02.pdf |archive-date=2010-06-10 }}</ref> Scafetta used this method in a 2002 analysis of teen pregnancy.<ref>{{cite news |author=Goforth, Sarah |date=August 12, 2002 |url=http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=DM&p_theme=dm&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=0F5644EC88CE040D&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&s_trackval=GooglePM |title=A new perspective on teen pregnancy: Mathematical approach clarifies subtle patterns, points way to action |work=[[Dallas Morning News]] |access-date=2012-08-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Ball, Philip |date=June 3, 2002 |url=http://www.nature.com/news/2002/020603/full/news020527-15.html |title=Less lovin' in summer: Texan teen conception rates linked to school term times |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |doi=10.1038/news020527-15 |access-date=2012-08-21|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Views on climate change==
Scafetta has argued, "At least 60% of the warming of the Earth observed since 1970 appears to be induced by natural cycles which are present in the solar system," instead claiming that climate  is modulated by astronomical oscillations. Scafetta's climate model is based primarily on a comparison of  periodic changes of [[global surface temperature]] and the Sun's periodic movement around [[Barycenter#Two-body problem|barycenter of the Solar System]], as well as solar, lunar, and planetary cycles.<ref>Nicola Scafetta, "Empirical evidence for a celestial origin of the climate oscillations and its implications," Journal of Atmospheric and Solar-Terrestrial Physics, 2010 '''72''', 951-970. [https://web.archive.org/web/20100610074216/http://www.fel.duke.edu/~scafetta/pdf/scafetta-JSTP2.pdf Full text]</ref>

In 2009, Scafetta faced criticism for failing to disclose the computer code required to reproduce his research.<ref name=lepage>{{cite web |author=Le Page, Michael |date=December 18, 2009 |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn18307-sceptical-climate-researcher-wont-divulge-key-program.html |title=Sceptical climate researcher won't divulge key program |work=[[New Scientist]] |access-date=2012-08-22}}</ref> Scafetta responded by saying that the code in question had been submitted to a scientific journal and that if "the journal takes its time to publish it, it is not our fault."<ref name=lepage/>

In a 2011 article published in ''The Open Atmospheric Science Journal'' ecologist Craig Loehle of the National Council for Air and Stream Improvement (a forest industry institution) and Scafetta forecast that the world climate "may remain approximately steady until 2030-2040, and may at most warm 0.5-1.0°C by 2100 at the estimated 0.66°C/century anthropogenic warming rate".<ref>Craig Loehle and Nicola Scafetta, "Climate Change Attribution Using Empirical Decomposition of Climatic Data," The Open Atmospheric Science Journal, 2011 '''5''', 74-86. [http://wattsupwiththat.files.wordpress.com/2011/07/loehlescafetta.pdf Full text] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210607052742/https://wattsupwiththat.files.wordpress.com/2011/07/loehlescafetta.pdf |date=2021-06-07 }}</ref>

In 2020, Scafetta proposed a 60-year cycle in the amount of interplanetary dust entering Earth's atmosphere, modulated by variations in the orbit of Jupiter's eccentricity, as causing variations in the relative abundance of cloud cover and thus being a driver of climate change by affecting variations in albedo.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Scafetta |first1=Nicola |last2=Milani |first2=Franco |last3=Bianchini |first3=Antonio |date=14 September 2020 |title=A 60-Year Cycle in the Meteorite Fall Frequency Suggests a Possible Interplanetary Dust Forcing of the Earth's Climate Driven by Planetary Oscillations |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2020GL089954 |journal=[[Geophysical Research Letters]] |volume=47 |issue=18 |doi=10.1029/2020GL089954 |bibcode=2020GeoRL..4789954S |s2cid=224921749 |access-date=23 November 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 2022, Scafetta wrote a paper claiming that equilibrium climate sensitivity was significantly lower than what Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (phase 6) (CMIP6) predict.<ref name="ScafettaCMIP6">{{cite journal |last1=Scafetta |first1=Nicola |date=18 September 2022 |title=CMIP6 GCM ensemble members versus global surface temperatures |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00382-022-06493-w |journal=[[Climate Dynamics]] |volume=60 |issue=9–10 |pages=3091–3120 |doi=10.1007/s00382-022-06493-w |access-date=20 March 2023|arxiv=2210.11414 }}</ref>
